latin.268:
ANNOTATIO V.
De Limitibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae ad pag. 347.–352.
latin.269:
§. I.
Limites, Obicibus oppositi, intelliguntur de Jure, uti Obices de facto. Quemadmodum limes injustus, obicis, ita obex justus, limitis naturam induit. Hinc limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae hoc loco intelliguntur, non quales actu & de facto dantur, sed quales jure, & quidem Divinô ac Ecclesiastico, dari & possent, & debent.
latin.270: Ita verò intellecti, vel sumuntur Materialiter, pro rebus, seu Articulis Christ. Religionis, Consociationem Ecclesiasticam juste limitantibus, seu ad justos terminos redigentibus, intraque eosdem continentibus; vel Formaliter pro limitatione ipsâ, seu actu limitandi vario graduque.
latin.271:
§. II.
Res Consociationem Ecclesiasticam limitantes, seu justos ei terminos figentes, non sunt Veritates Christianae quaecunque, sed Fundamentales, seu Fundamentalia Fidei Christianae dogmata, Annot. 2dâ descripta. Talia dari, ab aliis scilicet Fidei Christianae dogmatibus minùs fundamentalibus diversa, hisque contradistinguenda, probatum alibi, tùm ab Autore nostro Tract. de Fundamentalibus, Disp. 1. & 2. itemque Specim. Strict. contra Episcop. Condomiensem a. p. 63. ad 70. tùm à nobis, Dissert. de Pace Eccles. Cap. 7. & in Inquisit. in Arminianis. Annot. 17. omniumque Protestantium calculô confirmatum, etiam adversus Pontificios,
latin.272: Fundamentales, sive auctoritate Divinâ eâque immediatâ, sive naturâ suâ talia, quòd fidem Christianam fundant, per se agnoscentes nulla, omnia verò Dogmata fidei Christianae maxima minimaque, tùm quà Veritatem, tùm quà Necessitatem, aut Fundamentalitatem, ab Auctoritate Ecclesiae Romanae suspendentes, quâ fit, ut quod vel fidem Christianam contingit minimum, vel fidei Christianae adversum est, illud nihilominus, hôc non obstante, per Constantiense quoddam, vel Papale Concilium, fidei Christianae essentiale evadat vel maximum,
latin.273: eóque porrò illi, qui e. g. affirmat cum Paulo, in Eucharistiae Sacramento remanere substantiam Panis & Vini, 1. Cor. XI. 26. 27. 28. haut aliter, ac si fundamentum fidei Christianae integrum conculcâsset, anathema terribile per Concilium Tridentinum Session. XIII. Canon. II. annunciatum sit his verbis: Si quis dixerit, in Sacrosancto Eucharistiae Sacramento remanere Substantiam panis & vini unà cum Corpore & Sanguine Domini nostri Jesu Christi, negaveritque mirabilem illam & singularem Conversionem totius Substantiae panis in Corpus & totius substantiae vini in Sanguinem manentibus duntaxat Speciebus panis & vini: quam quidem Conversionem Catholica Ecclesia aptissimè Transsubstantiationem appellat, anathema sit. pag. m. 130.

pass_a.268:
ANNOTATION V.
On the Limits of Ecclesiastical Consociation, at pages 347–352.
pass_a.269: §. I. Limits, opposite to Obstacles, are understood of Right, as Obstacles are of fact. Just as an unjust boundary takes on the nature of an obstacle, so a just obstacle takes on the nature of a limit. Hence the limits of Ecclesiastical Consociation in this place are understood not such as are given in act and de facto, but such as by right — and indeed by Divine and Ecclesiastical right — both can and ought to be given.
pass_a.270: So understood, they are taken either Materially, for the things or Articles of the Christian Religion that justly limit Ecclesiastical Consociation, or reduce it to just bounds and keep it within them; or Formally, for the limitation itself, or the act of limiting in its various degree.
pass_a.271: §. II. The things limiting Ecclesiastical Consociation, or fixing just bounds for it, are not Christian Truths of every sort, but Fundamental ones, or the Fundamental dogmas of the Christian Faith, described in Annotation 2. That such are given, diverse from other less fundamental dogmas of the Christian Faith and to be contradistinguished from them, has been proved elsewhere — both by our Author in the Tract on Fundamentals, Disp. 1 & 2, and likewise Specim. Strict. against the Bishop of Condom, pp. 63–70; and by us in the Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Peace, Cap. 7, and in the Inquiry into the Arminians, Annot. 17 — and confirmed by the reckoning of all Protestants, even against the Pontificians,
pass_a.272: who acknowledge no Fundamentals in themselves — whether by immediate Divine authority or by their own nature as founding the Christian faith — but hang all Dogmas of the Christian faith, greatest and least, as to Truth, Necessity, or Fundamentality, upon the Authority of the Roman Church; whereby it comes about that what either touches the Christian faith least, or is adverse to the Christian faith, may nevertheless, this notwithstanding, through some Council of Constance or Papal Council become essential to the Christian faith, even the greatest,
pass_a.273: and so further that to him who, for example, affirms with Paul that in the Sacrament of the Eucharist the substance of Bread and Wine remains (1 Cor. 11:26–28), no otherwise than if he had trampled the whole foundation of the Christian faith, a terrible anathema has been announced by the Council of Trent, Session XIII, Canon II, in these words: If anyone shall say that in the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist the Substance of bread and wine remains together with the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and shall deny that marvelous and singular Conversion of the whole Substance of bread into the Body and of the whole substance of wine into the Blood, the species of bread and wine alone remaining — which Conversion the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation — let him be anathema. pag. m. 130.

268: Concerning the bounds of church Consociation — Autor pages 347 through 352.
269: §. I. Limits stand opposite Obstacles: limits are understood of right, obstacles of fact.
An unjust boundary acts like an obstacle; a just obstacle acts like a limit.
So here the limits of church consociation are not whatever happens to obtain in practice, but what by divine and church right can and ought to be set.
270: Taken that way, limits are either Material — the things or articles of the Christian religion that justly bound church consociation and keep it inside those bounds —
or Formal — the limitation itself, the act of limiting in its various degrees.
271: §. II. What sets just bounds for church consociation is not every Christian truth whatever, but the Fundamental dogmas of the Christian faith (described in Annotation 2).

That such fundamentals exist, distinct from less fundamental dogmas, has been shown elsewhere — by our Author’s Tract on Fundamentals (Disp. 1–2) and his Specimen against the Bishop of Condom (pp. 63–70), and by us in the Dissertation on Church Peace (ch. 7) and the Inquiry into the Arminians (Annot. 17) —
and all Protestants reckon the same way, even against the Roman party,
272: who own no fundamentals in themselves — neither by immediate divine authority nor by their nature as founding the Christian faith —
but hang every dogma of the faith, great or small, as to truth, necessity, or fundamentality, on the authority of the Roman Church.
So what barely touches the Christian faith, or even runs against it, can still, through some Constance or papal council, become essential to that faith — even the greatest point.
273: Thus someone who affirms with Paul that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine remains (1 Cor. 11:26–28) is treated no milder than if he had trampled the whole foundation of the Christian faith:

Trent, Session XIII, Canon II, launches a terrible anathema in these words — if anyone says the substance of bread and wine remains with Christ’s Body and Blood, and denies that marvelous conversion of the whole substance of bread into the Body and of wine into the Blood (species alone remaining), which the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation, let him be anathema (pag. m. 130).
Stop before the proof that true divine Fundamentals make the limits — from Ephesians 4 (authoritative and ratiocinative).
